title: How One Letter Changes a Protein

scenes.tts: Look at one spot in a hemoglobin gene. In most people, it reads G A G. In some people, it reads G T G. That one letter can bend a soft, round red blood cell into a stiff, curved sickle shape. How can one letter change a whole cell? The answer starts with how a cell uses a gene to make a protein.

scenes.tts: Making a protein from a gene is called protein synthesis. It has two stages. In plant and animal cells, the D N A stays in the nucleus, but proteins are built outside it. So the cell first makes a copy. Transcription is the first stage. An enzyme copies one gene into a strand of R N A. This copy is called messenger R N A.
scenes.caption: Making a protein from a gene is called protein synthesis. It has two stages. In plant and animal cells, the DNA stays in the nucleus, but proteins are built outside it. So the cell first makes a copy. Transcription is the first stage. An enzyme copies one gene into a strand of RNA. This copy is called messenger RNA.
scenes.visual: DNA stays in the nucleus; a copy is made as messenger RNA.
scenes.narration: Making a protein from a gene is called protein synthesis. It has two stages. In plant and animal cells, the DNA stays in the nucleus, but proteins are built outside it. So the cell first makes a copy. Transcription is the first stage. An enzyme copies one gene into a strand of RNA. This copy is called messenger RNA.

scenes.tts: The enzyme reads one D N A strand, and pairs a new R N A letter with each D N A letter. D N A letter A pairs with U. T pairs with A. C pairs with G. G pairs with C. R N A uses U where D N A uses T. Then the messenger R N A leaves the nucleus through pores.
scenes.caption: The enzyme reads one DNA strand, and pairs a new RNA letter with each DNA letter. DNA letter A pairs with U. T pairs with A. C pairs with G. G pairs with C. RNA uses U where DNA uses T. Then the messenger RNA leaves the nucleus through pores.
scenes.visual: Pairing DNA letters to RNA letters, then leaving through a pore.
scenes.narration: The enzyme reads one DNA strand, and pairs a new RNA letter with each DNA letter. DNA letter A pairs with U. T pairs with A. C pairs with G. G pairs with C. RNA uses U where DNA uses T. Then the messenger RNA leaves the nucleus through pores.

scenes.tts: Translation is the second stage. A ribosome in the cytoplasm reads the messenger R N A three letters at a time. Each group of three letters is a codon. Each codon stands for one amino acid, or for stop. Transfer R N A brings the matching amino acid. The ribosome joins the amino acids into a chain.
scenes.caption: Translation is the second stage. A ribosome in the cytoplasm reads the messenger RNA three letters at a time. Each group of three letters is a codon. Each codon stands for one amino acid, or for stop. Transfer RNA brings the matching amino acid. The ribosome joins the amino acids into a chain.
scenes.visual: A ribosome reads codons; tRNA brings amino acids; chain grows.
scenes.narration: Translation is the second stage. A ribosome in the cytoplasm reads the messenger RNA three letters at a time. Each group of three letters is a codon. Each codon stands for one amino acid, or for stop. Transfer RNA brings the matching amino acid. The ribosome joins the amino acids into a chain.

scenes.tts: The codon A U G stands for methionine, and it is the usual start. The codons G A G and G A A both stand for glutamic acid. U U U stands for phenylalanine. Then U G A means stop. It adds no amino acid, and the chain is released. The chain folds into a shape, and that shape lets the protein work.
scenes.caption: The codon AUG stands for methionine, and it is the usual start. The codons GAG and GAA both stand for glutamic acid. UUU stands for phenylalanine. Then UGA means stop. It adds no amino acid, and the chain is released. The chain folds into a shape, and that shape lets the protein work.
scenes.visual: Codons AUG GAG GAA UUU UGA become a chain; stop adds nothing.
scenes.narration: The codon AUG stands for methionine, and it is the usual start. The codons GAG and GAA both stand for glutamic acid. UUU stands for phenylalanine. Then UGA means stop. It adds no amino acid, and the chain is released. The chain folds into a shape, and that shape lets the protein work.

scenes.tts: Now back to hemoglobin. In the usual numbering, the sixth amino acid in its chain is glutamic acid, coded by G A G. In the sickle allele, the coding strand of the D N A reads G T G. The coding strand matches the messenger R N A, with T where the R N A has U. So the codon is G U G, and valine takes its place. Hemoglobin with valine can stick into stiff rods, mostly when oxygen is low. One changed letter can change one amino acid, and that can change a protein's shape.
